newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's successor faces bumpy start.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's successor faces bumpy start.

text.p: Mother Teresa's successor at the Missionaries of Charity could face a bumpy start as she emerges from the shadow of the charismatic Nobel peace laureate, nuns and church officials said at the weekend.
"It will take a while to get used to the fact that Mother Teresa is no longer the head," Father C. Bouche, spiritual adviser to the Missionaries of Charity, told Reuters.
"As in any new era, there will be some difficulty in the beginning but the order will adapt gradually to the change," said Father Bouche, who has worked with the order for 42 years.
Shy, softspoken Sister Nirmala, who was born a Hindu and later converted to Christianity, was unanimously elected to head the order by 132 senior nuns last week.
The election process would have been chaotic without Mother Teresa's presence, Father Bouche said.
Mother Teresa, who had headed the order since its creation in 1948, decided last year to step down after being taken to hospital three times for emergency care and undergoing heart surgery.

Nuns and volunteers at the Missionaries of Charity said Sister Nirmala had the advantage of Mother Teresa's constant guidance. The order says the 86-year-old nun will turn her administrative powers -- but not her title "Mother" -- over to her 63-year-old successor.
"For Sister Nirmala it will be a period of consolidation for the order rather than growth," Father Bouche said. She is due to visit many of the 568 homes run by the order in 120 countries.
Sister Nirmala, who opened the Missionaries of Charity's first overseas mission in Venezuela in 1965, has vast experience in running the order's homes, nuns said.
"She (Sister Nirmala) is very gentle but very firm. She doesn't hesitate in decision-making," said a volunteer, Sunita Kumar, who has been associated with the order for nearly three decades.
Kumar, who used to look after foreign volunteers visiting the Missionaries of Charity, said the flow of foreign donations to the order would not be affected by the change of leadership.
"It is Mother's work that draws foreign volunteers. I don't think that is going to stop," Kumar said.
But Father Bouche said he was unsure about how Western society would accept Sister Nirmala, who was born a high-caste Hindu and converted to Christianity at the age of 24.
"We have to wait and see," he said.
Her Hindu origins were not relevant to the order's nuns, many of whom were not even aware of them, he said.
"Mother always tells her nuns that God will take care of you if you remain one," Father Bouche said.

Last year, the Missionaries of Charity fed more than half a million people in some 111 countries. It teaches some 20,000 children in its schools and treats 90,000 lepers in its clinics. It also runs orphanages and homes for the dying.
The order guides hundreds of volunteers who queue up to face lives of hardship, apart from some 4,500 nuns around the world.
They live a life of personal deprivation. The only worldly possessions the charity's nuns may have are three saris, a spoon and plastic dish. They sleep on the floor.
"Sister Nirmala is very spiritual. Just like Mother. And she has the capability to hold the order together," Father Bouche said.
